item.title: Oct W1 26 - Spotlight: Rasa, Bhav and Abhinaya : A pathway to ‘Meditation in Motion’ (Radhika Gowardhan)
item.description:
Rasa, Bhav and Abhinaya : A pathway to ‘Meditation in Motion’ - Radhika Gowardhan - 2026 https://doi.org/10.67754/ijiis.special.edi2.vol02.0016
Abhinavdhara International Journal of Innovation in Indic Studies (2026). Dance is one of the earliest and most fundamental modes of human expression, emerging alongside the evolution of humanity as a means of communicating emotion through bhava and expression through rasa and abhinaya.From spontaneous movement to structured forms, dance has developed across countries in different forms and is part of human rituals, celebration and festivals.Rasa -The Sanskrit word for 'essence' can directly lead to a meditative state; by engaging deeply with the present moment through emotions, art, or sensory experiences, rasa serves as an entry point to calm the mind and enter a meditative state.Bhava -The Sanskrit word for feeling can naturally lead to meditation.By directing and channelising one's emotional energies by focussing on mind and transitions your awareness into a state of deep one-pointed concentration.Abhinaya -The art of dramatic expression and acting) can be a profound pathway to meditation both practices require intense present moment awareness breath control and the ability to detach from the ego to fully embody a subject.Thus, a combination of the three pillars of dancing rsa, bhava and abhinaya leads to a complete meditative state of the mind where there is a performer is only in the present and is without self-awareness and ego and had become one with character and the performance just flows though just like soft wind touches the nostril whole breathing.

item.title: Oct W1 26 - Spotlight: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Addressing Chronic Cancer Pain: A Narrative Review with Considerations for Utilization in Primary Care (Nina Hanenson Russin et al.)
item.description:
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Addressing Chronic Cancer Pain: A Narrative Review with Considerations for Utilization in Primary Care - Nina Hanenson Russin et al. - 2026 https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare14193232
Healthcare (2026). Background: Chronic pain is common among cancer survivors and may reflect interacting physical, psychological, social, and existential factors. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a behavioral intervention that emphasizes psychological flexibility, acceptance, present-moment awareness, and values-guided action. As cancer survivorship care increasingly involves primary care, scalable behavioral approaches may be needed to complement medical pain management, particularly where specialty behavioral health resources are limited. Methods: This narrative review examined evidence for ACT in chronic cancer-related pain and its potential applicability to primary care and resource-constrained healthcare settings. Searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, and CINAHL Ultimate, supplemented by Google Scholar and the Association for Contextual Behavioral Science database. Fifteen studies met criteria for inclusion. Results: ACT showed promising effects on outcomes including psychological flexibility, pain acceptance, emotional distress, quality of life, pain coping, and pain-related functioning, whereas findings for pain intensity were less consistent. The evidence was limited by heterogeneous study designs and populations and generally small experimental samples. None of the included studies directly evaluated ACT for cancer-related pain in primary care, although studies in other chronic pain and mental health populations provide indirect support for the feasibility of ACT in primary care and community settings. Discussion: Although direct evidence for the utilization of ACT in primary care is lacking, studies on ACT interventions for chronic pain and mental illness in these settings suggest that brief ACT interventions for cancer pain may help to address the need for behavioral health support. Future research should include pragmatic trials to determine whether brief ACT-informed interventions can be feasibly integrated into multidisciplinary primary care teams and delivered through digital or hybrid models.

item.title: Oct W1 26 - Spotlight: Associations between muscle dysmorphia symptoms and sexual functioning among sexually active boys and young men (Kyle T. Ganson et al.)
item.description:
Associations between muscle dysmorphia symptoms and sexual functioning among sexually active boys and young men - Kyle T. Ganson et al. - 2026 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bodyim.2026.102201
Body Image (2026). Muscle dysmorphia is characterized by a pathological pursuit of muscularity, pronounced body dissatisfaction, and functional impairment. Although muscle dysmorphia symptoms have been linked with numerous adverse health and psychosocial correlates, its association with sexual functioning among boys and young men remains underexplored. This study examined associations between muscle dysmorphia symptoms and sexual dysfunction among sexually active boys and men (N = 1116). Data were drawn from The Study of Boys and Men, an online survey of males aged 15-35 years recruited via social media advertisements in 2024. Muscle dysmorphia symptoms were assessed using the Muscle Dysmorphic Disorder Inventory (MDDI), and eight domains of sexual functioning (e.g., anxiety, lack of arousal, physical pain, erectile dysfunction) were assessed using items from the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles Sexual Functioning measure. Multiple logistic and linear regression models tested associations between MDDI scores (Drive for Size, Appearance Intolerance, Functional Impairment, and total score) and eight forms of sexual dysfunction, as well as an aggregate count of sexual dysfunction, adjusting for sociodemographic covariates. Greater muscle dysmorphia symptoms, particularly Appearance Intolerance and the MDDI total score, were consistently associated with a broad range of sexual dysfunction and a greater number of sexual dysfunctions. Drive for Size and Functional Impairment showed fewer, smaller, significant associations. These findings suggest that sexual dysfunction may co-occur with muscle dysmorphia among sexually active boys and young men, underscoring the importance of assessing and addressing sexual health within clinical and preventive interventions targeting boys' and men's body image.
